In the bustling streets of Navi Mumbai, India, a group of teenagers (mostly 17–18 years old) from the youth-led environmental team Urvari saw stray dogs struggling in the heavy monsoon rains. 

Determined to help, they collected plastic waste from their neighborhoods and created "eco-bricks" by tightly packing non-recyclable plastic bags and wrappers into used plastic bottles. It took around 150 of these sturdy "bottle bricks" (equivalent to about 40 kg of plastic) to build one durable, raised shelter—elevated off the wet ground, weather-resistant, and easy to place in parks or safe corners. 

They installed their first ones at places like Rajiv Gandhi Udyan, giving street dogs a dry, safe spot during the downpours. What started as a small Plastic Free July project showed how youth power and creativity can tackle two big problems at once: plastic pollution and animal suffering.

Meanwhile, in Zacatecas, Mexico, at the Zacatecas Educational Institute elementary school, 35 young students (guided by their teacher) launched a similar mission. They gathered recycled materials from home—plastic bottles, cardboard, old sheets, wood scraps, and cloth—and built cozy, insulated dog houses designed to protect stray dogs from cold nights and rain. 

The goal was double: create safe havens for abandoned animals and promote recycling in their community. Once finished, the children proudly donated the shelters to the local non-profit Albergues Lazos Caninos, a rescue group that cares for strays in the region. Their creative project went viral, inspiring others to see trash as treasure for helping voiceless creatures.

The monkey who refuses to leave Punch’s side has a name.
Go-chan.
Before he ever met Punch, Go-chan had his own battle to survive. He grew up in a circus, surrounded by noise, bright lights, and other monkeys who never truly accepted him. He didn’t fit in. He was bullied. The stress wore on his small body until it showed.
Eventually, he was moved to the zoo.
That’s where Punch was.
Punch, the little monkey who once clung to a toy because he had no one else. Punch, who sat alone even in a crowded troop.
And somehow… Go-chan was the first to walk up to him.
The first to sit close.
The first to reach out and hug him.
No hesitation. No fear.
Just understanding.
Maybe it’s because pain recognizes pain. Maybe it’s because the ones who know what loneliness feels like can spot it from a distance. Go-chan didn’t see a strange monkey. He saw a reflection.
Two souls who had both struggled to belong.
And instead of turning away, he chose to stay.
Their bond didn’t fade after that first embrace. It grew. They sit together. Move together. Support each other quietly, without needing attention.
It’s not loud. It’s not dramatic.
It’s steady.
And sometimes, that’s the most powerful kind of love.
The world can be harsh. Even for animals. Especially for the sensitive ones.
But every now and then, two wounded hearts find each other.
And instead of breaking again…
They heal together.
So if you see Punch, know he isn’t alone anymore.
Go-chan made sure of that. 🤍

HOW FREEMASONRY SHAPED IRAN

The political movement that culminated in Iran’s first constitution in 1906, and the creation of its first parliament, was driven by an intellectual transformation shaped in part by Freemasonic ideologies. 

How these ideas penetrated Iranian society, despite the country’s lack of a developed print culture, has long puzzled historians. One important conduit for their transmission was Freemasonry.

In 1835, three Iranian princes traveled to London, where they observed and reflected on the many notable changes underway in England. 

Their admiration for British ideas of "liberty" is evident throughout a diary they kept during the journey, with an entry dated 27 July standing out as particularly revealing:

"…went to a house in which the Lodge of Friendship of Freemasons was assembled. Here we had the honour to join the Lodge, where all of us too our first degree in this most noble society. Every man who desires to join in, must go himself and see. But I can say this, that it is a most honourable, desirable, and sacred secret. Every person that desires to become a member must be above the age of 22 years. No slave, nor woman is admissible… A person may take the three first degrees of Freemasonry, within a year and half, and a fourth after that period has elapsed."

"A freemason, after taking his degrees, will have a patent from the head of the society, signed by the noble, declaring him to be such. The head of all the freemasons in the world, is His Royal Highness, the Duke of Sussex, a brother of his Majesty."

- Travel diary (safar-nāmeh) of Reza Qoli Mirza Qajar, written during the 1835 visit of Qajar princes to Britain.
